description: Four-panel composite of tensile-test data for 20% cold-rolled (CR20%) low-density Fe-20Mn-9Al-1.2C-xCr steel strips, with curves colour-coded black = 0Cr, red = 3Cr, blue = 6Cr. (a) Engineering stress-strain curves of CR20%: y-axis "Engineering Stress/MPa" (0-1400), x-axis "Engineering Strain/%" (0-30); the 0Cr curve lies lowest with its plateau between the 1000 and 1200 MPa gridlines, while the 3Cr and 6Cr curves are close together and higher, between the 1200 and 1400 MPa gridlines; the 0Cr curve ends (fractures) near 22% strain and the 3Cr/6Cr curves near 23-24%. (b) Same axes for CR20% + annealed strips: shapes are similar, 0Cr remains lowest and 3Cr/6Cr highest, but all curves terminate at lower strain (roughly 19-20%). (c,d) Dual-axis plots for CR20% (c) and CR20% + annealed (d): left axis "True Stress/MPa" (0-1600) with solid curves, right axis "Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) MPa" (0-4000) with dashed curves, x-axis "True Strain" (0.00-0.25); black/red/blue arrows label the 0Cr/3Cr/6Cr curves. Two green dotted horizontal reference lines cross each panel. Solid true-stress curves saturate between the 1400 and 1600 MPa gridlines; dashed hardening-rate curves drop from the top of the 0-4000 range at low true strain and then decay, with 0Cr lowest. Overall the figure shows Cr addition raises the strength of cold-rolled strips while annealing does not remove that gain.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress-strain curves of CR20% steel strips (0Cr black, 3Cr red, 6Cr blue); axes Engineering Strain/% (0-30) vs Engineering Stress/MPa (0-1400). The 0Cr plateau is lowest (between the 1000 and 1200 MPa gridlines); 3Cr and 6Cr are higher and nearly overlapping (between 1200 and 1400 MPa); 0Cr terminates at lower strain (~22%) than 3Cr/6Cr (~23-24%).

Engineering stress-strain curves of CR20% + annealed steel strips with the same axes and colour coding. The ranking is unchanged (0Cr lowest, 3Cr slightly above 6Cr), but fracture/termination strain is lower, near 19-20% for 3Cr and 6Cr and about 20% for 0Cr.

Dual-axis plot for CR20%: solid true stress-true strain curves (left axis True Stress/MPa, 0-1600) with arrow labels pointing to the 0Cr, 3Cr and 6Cr curves, plus dashed strain hardening rate curves (right axis Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) MPa, 0-4000) versus True Strain (0.00-0.25). Two green dotted horizontal reference lines cross the panel.

Dual-axis plot for CR20% + annealed strips, same axes and colour/arrow labelling as (c). Dashed hardening-rate curves for 0Cr and 3Cr lie lower than in (c) at early strain, and the solid true-stress curves saturate below the 1600 MPa gridline; the two green dotted reference lines reappear.

observations.observation: In (a), the black 0Cr engineering stress-strain curve is the lowest of the three, with its plateau between the 1000 and 1200 MPa gridlines, while the red 3Cr and blue 6Cr curves plateau between the 1200 and 1400 MPa gridlines.
In (a) the 0Cr curve terminates at a lower engineering strain than the 3Cr and 6Cr curves, which extend to roughly 23-24% before the stress drops.
In (b) (CR20% + annealed) the same ranking is preserved - 0Cr lowest, 3Cr and 6Cr higher - but all three curves terminate at lower strain (about 19-20%) than in (a).

Panels (c) and (d) each use two y-axes: solid curves are true stress in MPa (0-1600, left) and dashed curves are strain hardening rate dσ/dε in MPa (0-4000, right), both plotted against true strain from 0.00 to 0.25.

In (c) and (d) the dashed strain hardening rate curves fall steeply from values near the top of the 0-4000 MPa range at true strain below about 0.03, then decay gradually; the black 0Cr curve lies lowest throughout.

Two green dotted horizontal reference lines cross panels (c) and (d); their heights lie near the 2000 MPa and the 1000-1100 MPa levels of the strain-hardening-rate axis (roughly the 800 MPa and 430 MPa levels of the true-stress axis).
In (c) and (d) the solid true-stress curves saturate between the 1400 and 1600 MPa gridlines at high true strain, with the 0Cr curve below the 3Cr and 6Cr curves.
Arrows labeled 0Cr (black), 3Cr (red) and 6Cr (blue) in panels (c) and (d) identify which solid true-stress curve and which dashed hardening-rate curve belongs to each steel.

The caption states the figure contains engineering stress-strain curves of CR20% (a) and CR20% + annealed (b) steel strips, and true stress-strain plus strain hardening rate curves of CR20% (c) and CR20% + annealed (d) steel strips.

The citing text states the ultimate tensile strength is 1154 MPa, 1270 MPa and 1264 MPa for the CR20% 0Cr, 3Cr and 6Cr steel strips respectively, and that yield strength also increases with Cr addition.
The citing text states that compared with the CR20% steel strips, the yield strength and ultimate tensile strength of the CR20% + annealed steel strips do not change significantly.
The citing text states that the strain hardening rates of the CR20% steel strips decrease gradually with increasing strain, and that Cr addition increases the strain hardening rate.
The citing text states that annealing makes the strain hardening rates of the CR20% + annealed 0Cr and 3Cr steel strips clearly decrease at the early stage compared with the CR20% strips.
The citing text attributes the higher strength of the Cr-containing cold-rolled strips to a higher density of slip bands that block dislocation motion after 20% cold rolling.
